After Trump's election as U.S. President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Following the new U.S. administration's assumption of office, U.S. policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—shifting from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which could have profound impacts on the global economic landscape. It is worth noting that with the accelerated pace of U.S. interest rate hikes, a stronger U.S. dollar, and the potential adoption of trade protectionist measures by the U.S., risks faced by emerging market economies have intensified. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates have risen in line with U.S. dollar interbank rates. Nonetheless, liquidity conditions remain sound, and overall loan growth further increased in the second half of 2016. Following the implementation of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment but has rebounded recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the potential for a faster-than-expected pace of U.S. interest rate hikes, as well as the broader impact of U.S. policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of significant capital outflows and the potential implications for Hong Kong's interest rates. After Trump's election as U.S. President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election outcome surprise the market, but the related market reactions were also unexpected. In particular, expectations that Trump's tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation measures would boost U.S. economic growth drove global stock markets higher. Following the new U.S. administration's assumption of office, U.S. policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—shifting from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which could have profound impacts on the global economic landscape. However, the market-anticipated Trump tax cuts may not produce the expected stimulus for U.S. economic growth. Especially as U.S. economic activity is already near its potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to U.S. economic growth but could exacerbate upside risks to U.S. inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen notably, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. At the same time, rising trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" situation for both the U.S. and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would distort markets, harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy, which is still recovering weakly. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows due to faster U.S. interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the U.S. dollar has increased. This could drag on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration and concerns over sharp energy price increases, the market has repriced inflation risks, leading to a broad and significant rise in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of U.S. interest rate expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The research results show that since the 2013 "taper tantrum," the impact of the U.S. Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and U.S. interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions would have significant effects on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016 as exports rebounded, but market volatility—such as currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region due to earlier concerns over potential policy changes by the new U.S. government—only gradually stabilized by early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but risks and uncertainties are both elevated. U.S. interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and increased financial market volatility could lead to tighter financial conditions. At the same time, the U.S. may adopt protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, though the actual impact remains unclear. In Mainland China, overall economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector business spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilization, uncertainties remain regarding the growth outlook. In particular, if the real estate market continues to cool amid the government's determination to curb housing price increases, the sector's contribution to growth may decrease this year. Meanwhile, the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-U.S. trade relations could increase short-term economic uncertainties. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the CFETS basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 as the U.S. dollar appreciated and U.S. interest rates rose, but appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilization in private sector economic activity, there are still some concerns about the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given the acceleration of M1 growth alongside a slowdown in M2 growth. Special Topic 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Special Topic 3 (see page 27) examines factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The research results indicate no evidence of a liquidity trap in the Mainland, and the main reasons for M1 growth significantly outpacing M2 are the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid money due to recent monetary easing, and increased economic uncertainty potentially boosting precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong's economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, goods export growth rose in line with improved regional trade flows, while service exports grew steadily with the recovery in trade-related and transport services. As goods and service imports grew faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With economic growth rising, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new U.S. administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. Amid pressures for U.S. dollar appreciation and expectations of faster U.S. interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support to the real economy, potentially leading to tighter local financial conditions, especially in the event of tail risks. Special Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index to help monitor local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum slightly accelerated in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to food price fluctuations and rising housing rents. With stable import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained broadly stable but occasionally weakened after the U.S. interest rate hike in December. The convertibility undertaking was not triggered. As the U.S. dollar appreciated, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate further increased. Due to the large monetary base, Hong Kong interbank interest rates remained low but rose from October onwards due to year-end funding demand and catching up with U.S. interest rate hikes. As a result, the average mortgage rate, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in mortgage lending, edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared to 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by stronger local economic activity and increased financing demand from multinational corporations at year-end. Local loan growth slightly accelerated, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decline in the first half. By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded 3.2% growth as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. Bank funding conditions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at end-2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the U.S. dollar loan-to-deposit ratio declined significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in U.S. dollar deposits. Due to the strong U.S. dollar, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool (including customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances) further consolidated alongside other offshore renminbi markets, and volatility in offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rates increased significantly. Nonetheless, banks' renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi real-time gross settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is likely to continue facing headwinds from uncertainties in renminbi exchange rate trends. With improved global market conditions, Hong Kong's stock market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the U.S. presidential election yielded an unexpected result, the market was only briefly impacted. This was mainly due to investor optimism about fiscal stimulus measures under the Trump administration, which drove global stock markets higher. While benefiting from this, the Hong Kong market was also cautious amid optimism, possibly due to concerns over faster U.S. interest rate hikes, challenges in the Mainland economic outlook, renminbi policy uncertainties, and capital flow controls. Looking ahead, although the Hong Kong market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply at the end of last year and the spread with U.S. Treasury bonds widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar bond market expanded steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, but new bond issuance for the full year was still lower than the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets could face pressure. As U.S. trade policy remains unclear and the renminbi exchange rate may continue to be volatile, the outlook for these two bond markets over the next six months will remain clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the government's introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment but has rebounded recently. Given renewed market exuberance, the government raised the stamp duty uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the following two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting developers increasing the launch of primary units. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, but the pace of increase has slowed.

After Donald Trump's unexpected election as President of the United States, policy uncertainty in the US has increased. Although market focus is concentrated on the short-term benefits of potentially implemented large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is currently close to its economic potential. Fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth but will further exacerbate upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing due to capital outflow pressures from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures will also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with recent export volumes also increasing. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are expected to remain volatile, with downside risks to economic growth rising. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector business spending. The mainland economy continues to rebalance, with steady expansion in the tertiary sector, but ongoing economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb housing price rises, if the real estate market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate sector to economic growth may also decrease this year. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the CFETS basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased at the end of 2016 with the strengthening of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as market expectations that Trump would implement tax reforms, massively increase infrastructure spending, and deregulate policies would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating major stock markets to rise (Figure 2.1). Consequently, market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes heated up, causing US Treasury bond yields to surge and the US dollar to strengthen. Figure 2.1 Stock Market Indices of Some Advanced Economies However, the anticipated Trump tax cuts may not have the positive impact on US economic growth that markets expect. While shifting economic policy to rely on fiscal easing could help alleviate the heavy burden of monetary easing, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the February unemployment rate is in line with the Federal Reserve's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, where the fiscal multiplier is lower than during a recession (e.g., see Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labor or capital could lead to reduced tax revenue (e.g., see Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with reduced excess capacity, any measures to further boost economic growth, even if their real impact on growth is limited, could push up inflation. Meanwhile, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, and potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. Even as the risk of rising US inflation increases, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-loose monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risk. Since the US election, although market forecasts for the future federal funds rate have been revised up to near the median of the Federal Reserve's forecasts for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Fed's long-term forecast (Figure 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger risks of significant market volatility. While financial markets focus on the short-term benefits of potentially implemented expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures driving stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US national debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfill its campaign promises by adopting trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future Federal Funds Rate Forecasts: Federal Reserve vs. Market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and obstacle to the European economic recovery. Although the eurozone's economic environment is gradually improving, with real GDP in Q4 growing modestly by 1.7% year-on-year, slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year growth in Q3, eurozone economic activity remains only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels compared to the stronger recovery in the US (Figure 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, markets have been concerned about the eventual disintegration of the eurozone. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilized after forming a new government and implementing measures to rescue its banking sector, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe have continued to rise, and corporate bond spreads have widened, particularly in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and possibly putting pressure on business real investment in the eurozone. Figure 2.3 Real GDP of Major Advanced Economies In Japan, real GDP has been revised upward in recent quarters, with Q4 2016 annual growth increasing to 1.6% year-on-year, the fastest pace since Q3 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected economic recovery. However, partly due to structural issues in the labor market, wage growth has been slow, leading to weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent sharp depreciation of the yen suggests that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation from the earlier yen appreciation is about to begin receding. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improvement in the short-term inflation outlook. Although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations remain around 0.5%–0.6%, lower than levels at the launch of Abenomics in early 2014, so the risk of inflation failing to reach the Bank of Japan's 2% medium-term target persists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth through trade channels may be smaller, given the decline in US imports after the global financial crisis and the potential implementation of protectionist policies by the US. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will tighten financial conditions, exacerbating downside risks to the economy. This could drag on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion under the Trump administration, coupled with concerns about sharp rises in energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP growing modestly and inflation rising. Real GDP Growth – In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable as private consumption was steady in many regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally rose slightly from their low levels in 2015. This benefited not only from China's stabilized growth but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (e.g., Malaysia and Indonesia), the rebound in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained momentum due to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation – With the rebound in commodity prices, especially oil, producer price inflation generally showed an upward trend. While this will push up industrial costs and even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may increase due to reduced long-term deflation risks. Faster producer price inflation could put upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for CPI indicate that inflation in many regional economies, while still slightly below central banks' 2017 inflation targets, will rise closer to target levels (Figure 2.4). Except for Indonesia, where the central bank cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth, central banks in East Asia generally maintained accommodative monetary policy unchanged. Figure 2.4 Headline CPI Inflation, Forecasts, and Central Bank Targets in East Asia Despite improvements in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 led to short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign Exchange Markets – After the US election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated less or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Figure 2.5). Figure 2.5 Changes in Spot FX Depreciation Against the US Dollar and Nominal Effective Exchange Rates After the US Election Bond and Stock Markets – Asset prices briefly fell after the US presidential election but quickly stabilized. The spreads of sovereign bonds in East Asian economies over US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilized, yields in some regional economies fell but have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Figure 2.6 10-Year Sovereign Bond Spreads Over US Treasury Bonds Portfolio Investment Flows – Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in Q4 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. In the first few weeks of 2017, inflows resumed, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain stable but at a pace still below historical averages. Given heightened uncertainty over US government policies and the potential policy response from the Federal Reserve, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields could attract funds from the region to the US, leading investors to reduce holdings of regional assets, particularly those with already high valuations. Tightening financial conditions under such circumstances would also put repayment pressure on companies with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. On a macro level, a general global rise in interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, not only dragging on aggregate demand in the short term but also potentially affecting potential growth in the long term. Finally, export-oriented countries in the region face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies from the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has been widening in recent years (Figure 2.7), especially in the region's major export industries such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, clothing, and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries have led to significant job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose significant risks to the region's exporting countries.

Private consumption growth accelerated and public-sector building and construction activities were buoyant, leading to a slight pickup in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to an increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and a stable labor market, private consumption growth accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the Hong Kong International Airport's third runway, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, weak corporate capital expenditure narrowed the contribution of overall investment spending to GDP growth. Externally, both merchandise exports and imports accelerated in line with the rise in regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). Trade-related and transport services drove further growth in service exports, while service imports rebounded partly due to strong demand for outbound travel by local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components Chart 3.2 Real Exports and Imports The labor market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters, then edged down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major industries declined in the second half of the year, including retail, accommodation, and food services, partly due to a stabilization of the slowdown in the retail sector. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment Rate and Total Employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth may continue to be moderate. Coupled with the rise in the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate due to the strong US dollar, Hong Kong's export performance will be dampened. On the domestic front, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, dragged down by rising interest rates. With an increase in housing supply and the launch of several infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2017, while private sector analysts' average forecast is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly from the external environment. Policy uncertainties under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and potential protectionist trade policies could hinder global trade flows. The process of Brexit and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Additionally, US interest rate normalization will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation has remained generally moderate, despite a pickup in quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index stabilized at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, reflecting inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, then eased slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly driven by increases in tradable goods prices and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by basic food and clothing prices. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, as the decline in private residential rentals narrowed and public housing rents were raised in September 2016, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index increased, but subsequently eased slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer Price Inflation by Major Component Chart 3.6 Composite CPI Rental Component and Market Rentals In the short term, with weak import prices and moderate local cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. As the strong Hong Kong dollar partly offsets the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap is estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures, thereby curbing inflation in the services component. Although the labor market is tight, wage increases have been modest in recent quarters, with real per capita wages rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 and then falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the persistent uncertainties in the external environment leading to cautious business sentiment, the increase in labor costs should be restrained in this context. Furthermore, due to lackluster retail sales in recent months, retail property rental increases are expected to be moderate. Moreover, the gradual impact of earlier declines in private residential rentals will also help ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline for the full year of 2017, with the government forecasting an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the year, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and Import Prices Chart 3.8 Unit Labor Cost and Real Per Capita Wages The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation accelerates under the Trump administration in the US, it could lead to a faster pace of US interest rate hikes than expected, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak and also reduce Hong Kong's attractiveness to inbound tourists. On the upside, if global economic expansion is faster than expected, it could accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. Additionally, the upward adjustment of the statutory minimum wage, effective from May 1, 2017, could further increase inflation, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates rose in line with US dollar interbank rates. Overall loan growth continued to be moderate, partly due to improvements in the local economic environment. Looking ahead, with the pace of US interest rate normalisation accelerating, uncertainties surrounding the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. Despite financial market volatility, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to a general decline in Asian currencies, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections announced by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13-14 December 2016 fuelled market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken temporarily thereafter. At the beginning of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening from mid-February as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators With the strength of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of narrowing inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners was mild, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics show that non-resident investment in equities and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a large number of initial public offering activities (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, debt investment by residents recorded substantial outflows, which outweighed the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds showed portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly due to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, which put pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicate that Hong Kong portfolio investment experienced inflow pressures in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to improved global financial market performance as investors became optimistic about expansionary fiscal policies in the US. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the UK's exit from the European Union, and elections in EU member states could lead to increased volatility in fund flows. Additionally, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets could exert inflow pressures on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading volumes exceeded southbound trading volumes in the initial period following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under this scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained sizeable, rising further by 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within this, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly, due to the issuance of an additional HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' substantial demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base With the gradual stabilisation of the local economy, the growth of Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) picked up from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand due to stronger local economic activity and a rebound in initial public offering activities. Analysed by corresponding assets, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money creation from credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a higher growth rate of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in Renminbi deposits. Overall, total deposits of authorised institutions increased to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with full-year growth at 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale funding costs rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates remained low, they increased partly due to year-end funding demand and catching up with the rise in US dollar interbank interest rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half, to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward in line with the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at end-December. At the beginning of 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally fell as funding demand decreased, while long-term Hong Kong Government Bond yields also edged down in line with US Treasury yields. Banks' average funding cost (as measured by the Composite Interest Rate) remained low, rising by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). With relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage rate for new loans fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017, following the rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates. Driven by stronger local economic activity and higher cross-border financing demand, overall loans rose further by 4.2% in the second half, following a 2.2% increase in the first half (Chart 4.10). With rising economic growth momentum, local loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2%, as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. For the full year of 2016, overall loans grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Loans to the financial and related corporate sectors and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, to some extent reflecting strong financing demand driven by better growth prospects in these industries. Loans to the construction and property development sectors also accelerated in line with increased private construction activity. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Within household debt, partly reflecting improved economic conditions, personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal purpose loans) rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11), while residential mortgage loan growth accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting the buoyant residential property transactions from July to October. As a result, the ratio of household debt to Gross Domestic Product also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at end-June 2016 to 77.1% at end-December (Chart 4.13); meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at end-December, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio declining significantly to 63.8%, due to strong US dollar deposit growth. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Opinion Survey" indicates that loan demand remains soft in the near term. Due to the appreciation of the US dollar, both offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore Renminbi exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore rate for most of the latter part of 2016, closing at a year-low of 6.98 against the US dollar at end-2016. The offshore Renminbi interbank market experienced renewed liquidity tightening pressures in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate surged to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The subsequent rise in offshore Renminbi funding costs led to the covering of short positions in the offshore Renminbi, driving a rebound in the offshore Renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017, and the spread between the offshore and onshore Renminbi turned to a premium. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, and liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and three-month offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates falling to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively by end-February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared to the same period in 2015, driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. The capital position and asset quality of banks also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained favorable. The funding costs of retail banks stayed stable and low, supported by a large retail deposit base. However, banks should carefully assess the impact of potentially faster-than-expected US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of significant capital outflows and their subsequent potential impact on Hong Kong interest rates. Furthermore, given the continued rise in leverage levels of non-local corporates, a substantial increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks' asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer requirement will be raised to 1.875% effective from January 1, 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Figure 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. For the full year of 2016, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets increased from 1.05% in the full year of 2015 to 1.10%. Figure 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Wholesale funding costs in Hong Kong rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December 2016. Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate increased significantly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest Rates However, the overall impact of US interest rate hikes on the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained modest. As the primary funding source for retail banks is retail deposits, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low despite the rate hike, the Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, remained at a low level of around 0.26% for over a year before edging up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016. At a broader level, a similar situation was observed for the total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. While the average non-deposit market Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, at only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 17 basis points (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks The rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate exceeded and outpaced the increase in funding costs for Hong Kong banks, which could benefit some retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate-based mortgage loans in recent years, and the rise in interest rates on such loans may help expand their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there are signs that some banks have reduced their mortgage rate spreads relative to the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the long run, as the US further raises interest rates, banks may soon face pressure to increase retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and having a more significant impact on net interest margins. Banks' capital levels remained strong and well above international minimum requirements. During the reporting period, the asset quality of the retail bank loan portfolio remained sound. Banks' expectations for short-term credit growth varied. A sensitivity test showed that, if interest rates rose by 300 basis points while other conditions remained unchanged, the index could rise significantly to 67.3 within four quarters. 48 Banks should remain vigilant about the risks associated with the continued rise in individual debt burdens. As the market reassesses inflation risks in the United States, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. In February, global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely erasing the significant gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield rose to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global stock markets over the past two years with low volatility was driven by market expectations of continued robust economic growth, low inflation, and low interest rates. However, these expectations are now facing risks from tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall loan growth continued but at a slower pace. After a moderate slowdown in the middle of the year, property price increases and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in capital flows into Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy, and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant about the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and high levels of personal debt, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality if interest rates rise more than expected. After the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) had lingered at low levels for over two years, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global stock markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 index at one point dropping over 10%, completely erasing the significant gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was due to signs that the global economic recovery could put pressure on US wages and prices, which had been low for a long time, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global stock markets over the past two years was based on market expectations of continued favourable economic conditions. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with economic activity in both advanced and emerging market economies picking up simultaneously. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform plan, including tax cuts and comprehensive reforms to corporate and individual tax regulations, leading markets to anticipate additional cyclical stimulus to the strong US economic recovery in the short term. Despite the strengthening activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations of prolonged low global interest rates. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US stock markets repeatedly hitting new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global stock markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy more quickly. At the same time, as tax cuts lead to a higher fiscal deficit, the US may issue more government bonds in the future, which is expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to normalise its balance sheet. Outside the US, the strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a simultaneous tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cast a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to protect domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These actions raise concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in global financial markets. Given these uncertainties in the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the currently high valuations of global asset markets is questionable. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expected rise in the fiscal deficit due to US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*). Additionally, the normalisation of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which could push up long-term interest rates, thereby adversely affecting asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies are also in a favourable environment of robust growth and moderate inflation. With strong economic performance and optimistic prospects, capital inflows have accelerated, and financial markets have risen simultaneously. However, these favourable prospects face downside risks from the simultaneous normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks leading to a tightening of global liquidity; the US government's inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore dollar liquidity due to large-scale profit repatriation by US companies in response to the one-time "deemed repatriation" provision under the US tax reform. Any shocks to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with industries and economies with higher leverage being most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year, the Mainland Chinese economy performed well in the second half of 2017. At the same time, signs of the emergence of the "new economy" have become more apparent, with industries such as high value-added manufacturing and services showing strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive but with uncertainties. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from further structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which could help mitigate adverse economic changes if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, with the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland's real estate market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened loan approval standards, bank exposures to enterprises in overcapacity industries remained under control, while shadow banking activities slowed down amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints on state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capacity seem to have tightened, possibly due to reduced support from local governments (see Feature 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, with the stabilisation of the economic situation and reduced risks, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment spending also rebounded due to increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved. Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods still dragged on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports will continue to support economic growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Feature 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage payment burdens on private consumption. The government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are 3-4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the aforementioned external environment, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the trend of local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained under control. However, there are signs of a slight uptick in quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum in recent months, with prices of both traded goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up slightly to a still moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising rents for newly signed private residential properties. Affected by funding needs for IPO activities and seasonal funding demand, liquidity conditions tightened, and short Hong Kong dollar positions were covered, leading to a strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened again from December 2017 onwards. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets, particularly stock markets, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the convertibility undertaking was not triggered. Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates came under upward pressure between September and December 2017. This was mainly due to funding needs for IPO activities and banks' cautious liquidity management towards the year-end. In December, the average overnight and 3-month HIBOR rates were 0.25% and 1.26%, respectively, up 14 and 50 basis points from six months earlier. After easing slightly in early January 2018, HIBOR rates remained broadly stable, unaffected by the recent global financial market adjustments. Despite intense competition in the mortgage loan business, the average interest rate on newly approved mortgages by banks followed the rise in short-term HIBOR rates, reaching 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks' funding costs remained generally low after a brief spike in October due to IPO activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; if global financial market sentiment changes sharply, the volatility of capital flows could increase. For the full year of 2017, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. After strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. The growth rates of most local loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong declined. Foreign currency loan growth slowed, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. In contrast, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to record rapid growth, supported by the favourable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at the end of the year, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, due to relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the end of the year. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore renminbi strengthened against the US dollar from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool (including total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) rebounded slightly in the second half of the year after a small decline in the first half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations for the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi businesses, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the volume of renminbi trade settlement handled by Hong Kong banks rebounded in the second half of the year. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the "Belt and Road" initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global stock markets to sustained highs in 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, a sell-off and significant volatility in global stock markets in February marked the end of two years of calm in financial markets. Looking ahead, risks of tighter global financial conditions, along with a series of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In a tight labor market, US tax cuts may accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to normalize its balance sheet, increased US Treasury issuance to finance the tax cuts could add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The shadow of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, despite the optimistic economic outlook, it also faces multiple downside risks, such as a potentially greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, US inward-looking trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. The materialization of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on one hand, they must guard against risks to economic growth, while on the other, they need to limit the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and curbing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive but is subject to uncertainties, which will partly depend on the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can offset the short-term growth pressures from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilized and risks diminished, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. With the momentum of cyclical economic improvement becoming more entrenched since late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the US saw robust increases in investment and exports, driven by improved private sector sentiment and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the Eurozone and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilizing global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following the US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. Given the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of the US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1 Real GDP Growth Forecasts As growth momentum strengthened in the Eurozone and Japan, market expectations of a narrowing divergence in global monetary policy, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, spurred a rise in risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite the Federal Reserve raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to normalize its balance sheet, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks' targets, leading markets to expect, until recently, that global interest rates would remain low (Figure 2.2). Against this backdrop, global stock markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 index repeatedly hitting new highs, pushing its cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Figure 2.2 Core Inflation in Major Advanced Economies However, since the second half of 2017, concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher fiscal deficits and inflation have caused US long-term Treasury yields to rise steadily, raising questions about the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. Following the release of US data for January 2018 showing higher-than-expected average hourly earnings growth, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a global stock market correction in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index fell more than 10% from its January 26 peak, completely erasing its significant gains from the start of the year, and continued to face pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protectionist measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the CBOE Volatility Index spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the narrow trading range environment that had persisted for the previous two years (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields, and potential monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision aimed at reducing the incentive for US companies to park overseas profits abroad. Although it is not yet certain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output beyond its potential, leading to an overheating economy and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, it could prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Currently, financial markets anticipate a flatter path for the federal funds rate compared to the projections released by the Federal Reserve. However, if inflation surprises to the upside, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 Federal Funds Rate Forecasts Second, given that the tax reform is likely to exacerbate fiscal deficits, an increase in US Treasury issuance is expected in the future. As the Federal Reserve continues with its balance sheet normalization plan, which is expected to lead to a rise in term premiums, the increased supply of US Treasuries could add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Furthermore, as market expectations of the likelihood of US tax cuts passing increased, US inflation expectations have been rising since the second half of 2017 (Figure 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by over 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting concerns over increased Treasury supply pressure and rising inflation expectations. Figure 2.5 5-Year, 5-Year Forward Inflation Expectation Rate Additionally, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for an extended period as most expect. Although estimates of R* vary, it is widely believed to have fallen significantly since the global financial crisis (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the US R* may face upside risks in the future due to (1) an expected decline in the national saving rate resulting from higher fiscal deficits, and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate driven by corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment of capital expenditures. A rise in R*, along with the expected increase in term premiums from the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalization, could signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby posing headwinds to asset market valuations. Figure 2.6 US R* Estimated Using the Laubach-Williams Model Third, the strengthening growth momentum in the Eurozone and Japan has led markets to anticipate that their central banks may scale back monetary accommodation. If this occurs, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Eurozone, member economies experienced a broad-based cyclical expansion (Figure 2.7). In Japan, the economy also accelerated its recovery, with real GDP posting its eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continue to signal accommodative monetary policy amid subdued inflation, the improving economic growth outlook in Europe and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan's labor market) has led some market participants to predict a further reduction in their quantitative easing programs in the near future. The US government appears more inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries. Recent examples include the imposition of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines announced in January 2018, and the announcement of import tariffs on steel and aluminum in early March, raising concerns about potential retaliatory measures from its trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the UK and other EU countries regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements are ongoing, with multiple uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they could hinder global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions (such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East, and latent terrorist attack risks) could increase volatility in global financial markets. In East Asia, economic growth momentum further strengthened in the second half of 2017, concluding the year with a strong performance. The accelerated recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted exports from the region. With robust domestic demand and improved export performance, Hong Kong's economy maintained steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018. Hong Kong's economic outlook continues to be affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policies by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. Hong Kong's economy maintained growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the previous two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow steadily and remained a key driver of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust, supported by favourable employment and income conditions, still optimistic consumer sentiment, and positive effects from rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rise in overall investment spending in the final quarter, after three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as import growth outpaced export growth, net exports of goods still dragged on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components Chart 3.2 Real Exports and Imports Sustained economic growth momentum led to an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by about 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most notable increases in the construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain steady in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from improved global economic growth prospects and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and ongoing infrastructure projects. Although an improved economic environment will stimulate business capital expenditure, the potential rise in interest rates may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3 to 4% in 2018, while international institutions and private sector analysts forecast growth of 2 to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the economic performance of Mainland China under tightening financial conditions in the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, and the trend of local asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but month-on-month inflation momentum showed slight signs of picking up in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Among these, prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in newly signed private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures continued to remain moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.4 Rental Component of Composite CPI and Market Rents Chart 3.5 Unit Labour Cost and Per Capita Salary As global inflation remains moderate and local cost increases are stable, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, due to the pass-through effect from the growth in newly signed private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018. The market consensus forecasts overall inflation at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, any unexpected rise in global inflation or commodity prices could increase local inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has further tightened recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, the first time below 3% in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6).
