The current output gap is estimated to be near zero, and if the labour market tightens significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment Rate After the 2008 global financial crisis, interest rates were low, and Hong Kong households increased their mortgage debt. As US dollar interest rates normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow suit, leading to an increase in future household mortgage repayment burdens, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this box studies the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt service payments (i.e., interest payments plus loan principal repayments) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and wealth and collateral effects from asset price changes mentioned in general economic theory, under the presence of a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments, thereby altering household disposable income. This impact will increase with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans. Furthermore, loan principal repayments change with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, which also affects private consumption by changing household disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of Private Consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the outstanding mortgage debt service ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike current mortgage repayment burden indicators that only apply to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of households, which is more closely related to total private consumption. We broadly followed the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, using a standard fixed-instalment formula to measure the OMDSR: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (measured by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median mortgage repayment and loan repayment-to-income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the five-yearly population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing after the property market bubble burst in 1997 and the significant decline in mortgage interest rates during the same period. Despite a substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, these two ratios remained stable, as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's macroprudential measures on bank mortgage lending curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of the maturity of newly originated mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and Median Mortgage Repayment and Loan Repayment-to-Income Ratio We also compared the OMDSR with banks' debt service-to-income ratio, which is the actual debt service-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt service-to-income ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only newly originated mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e., banks' debt service-to-income ratio). Furthermore, banks' debt service-to-income ratio is also higher because banks comply with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements, which include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the debt service-to-income ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt service-to-income ratio remained stable, mainly due to the HKMA's prudential regulation of mortgage lending, which set a cap on banks' debt service-to-income ratio, and this measure also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and Banks' New Mortgage Debt Service-to-Income Ratio Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used repayment burden indicators, but the OMDSR has greater timeliness and can reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage debt, not just that of newly originated mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that using the OMDSR can assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the approach of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (measured by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we include real income (measured by median household income, deflated by the composite CPI), real housing and financial wealth (measured by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, deflated by the composite CPI), and the OMDSR as long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment shifts sharply, capital flow volatility could increase. In the second half of 2017, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot rate briefly strengthened and remained around 7.80 from September to November 2017. This was mainly due to increased demand for funds from IPO activities and banks' cautious liquidity management at month-end and year-end, leading to tighter liquidity conditions, which in turn slowed interest rate arbitrage activities and increased the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As the tightness in Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased and US dollar commercial demand rose at year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly stock markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the convertibility undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated modestly in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar further weakened (Chart 4.3). This is broadly consistent with the trend of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners is very small and has limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track movements in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Non-resident portfolio investments recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that in the third quarter, both resident and non-resident portfolio investments in equities recorded inflows, reflecting improved regional economic prospects and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-resident debt securities investments recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from resident debt investments. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, driven by optimism about economic prospects and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data indicated that despite adjustments in global financial markets, equity investments still recorded inflows, while bond investments saw slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market Survey of Equity and Bond-Related Capital Flows Looking ahead, as the normalization of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. At the same time, given the uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalization and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar capital flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully ensure the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Fed's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base further increased by 1.4%, mainly driven by the growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged in the second half, at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Among these, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite the stock market adjustment, the monetary base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKDM3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKDM3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to increased investment demand amid buoyant asset markets. An analysis of corresponding assets shows that the growth of HKDM3 was supported on one hand by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), and on the other hand dragged down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKDM3 and Its Corresponding Assets On the other hand, foreign currency deposit growth was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, which had been declining for over two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in Renminbi deposits. Due to the slowdown in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposit growth, total deposits of authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth Between September and December 2017, increased demand for funds from IPO activities and banks' cautious liquidity management at month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative interest rate differentials between 1-month and 3-month HIBOR and US dollar LIBOR correspondingly narrowed. Chart 4.8 HIBOR and US Dollar LIBOR At the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with the trend of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at end-2017, while the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rose by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Mortgage Rate for New Loans Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, HIBOR fell in early January. Thereafter, despite adjustments in global and local stock markets, HIBOR remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose with the spike in HIBOR, banks' funding costs generally remained low due to the still large deposit base. Despite intense competition in mortgage lending, the average mortgage rate for new loans gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the uptrend in the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Composite Interest Rate, which measures the cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, remained soft for most of the second half, despite a brief uptick in October due to increased demand for funds from IPO activities, closing at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalize and other major economies may also initiate interest rate normalization, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, volatile global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions could increase capital flow volatility. However, the large Hong Kong dollar monetary base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate any sharp rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Additionally, banks' prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window can also help curb excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate was as high as 10.2% in the first half, slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong both moderated. By currency, due to the favorable local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Among these, US dollar loan growth slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. For the full year of 2017, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan Growth The growth of loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade finance) slowed from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth for construction, property development, and investment slowed in the second half, partly due to the requirement since June 2017 for banks to strengthen risk management of loans to property developers. Despite further improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and transport sector loans recorded only relatively modest growth, while wholesale and retail trade loans declined. In contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related corporates remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Sectoral Breakdown of Domestic Loan Growth Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, the growth of personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal purpose loans) accelerated further, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management clients secured by financial assets. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth of client assets under management by banks. The risks of such secured loans are manageable. Furthermore, in January 2014, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on risk management for personal loans, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt servicing ratios. On the other hand, although residential property transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratio for new mortgage approvals declined, and the growth of residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Credit growth, after experiencing strong expansion in the first half of 2017, moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates, the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained low due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should be vigilant about the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows under the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. With corporate leverage continuing to rise and personal debt burdens remaining high, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality from interest rate increases exceeding expectations. To enhance banks' resilience to systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% effective from January 1, 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% year-on-year. This was mainly driven by a significant increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down to 1.15% in the second half of 2017 from 1.17% in the first half. Nonetheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.1). For the full year of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Figure 5.1 Retail Bank Profitability The net interest margin of retail banks further widened to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.2). Observational evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margin is consistent with the rise in the average spread of Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Figure 5.3 Average Spread of Hong Kong Dollar Syndicated Loans Since September 2017, Hong Kong interbank interest rates have risen across the board, mainly driven by liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and banks' near-year-end needs, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Among these, the 3-month Hong Kong interbank offered rate recorded a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up 53 basis points from the end of June, but still low by historical standards (blue line in Figure 5.4). Entering 2018, Hong Kong interbank interest rates appeared to stabilize as banks' year-end liquidity demand eased. Despite the recent rise in Hong Kong interbank interest rates, the Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Under these circumstances, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, remained low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before rising slightly to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Figure 5.4). A similar situation was observed for the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average non-deposit market Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks rose by 35 basis points, while average deposit funding costs increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Figure 5.5). Figure 5.4 Interest Rates Figure 5.5 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks The rise in Hong Kong interbank interest rates exceeded the overall funding cost increase of the Hong Kong banking industry, which may help improve the spreads on banks' assets benchmarked to Hong Kong interbank offered rates. However, this improvement may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data shows that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater pressure from rising funding costs. In light of intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above international minimum standards, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector maintains strong capital. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Figure 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Figure 5.6 Capital of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions The Hong Kong Monetary Authority recently published a consultation paper on formulating rules for the loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions can help reduce the likelihood of financial crises, thereby benefiting society, it inevitably incurs costs. Special Topic 5 conducts a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements will bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average liquidity coverage ratio of Class 1 institutions rose to 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 144.2% in the second quarter (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable for 2017. Although the average liquidity maintenance ratio of Class 2 institutions edged down to 49.4% in the fourth quarter from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector can withstand liquidity shocks resulting from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on January 1, 2018. This requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Class 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remain the main funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of total liabilities of all authorized institutions, roughly unchanged from six months earlier (Figure 5.8). Figure 5.8 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose to 82.7% at the end of December 2017 from 77.1% at the end of June (Figure 5.9), reflecting that Hong Kong dollar loans and advances grew faster than deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at the end of December from 65.5% at the end of June 2017. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months earlier. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Figure 5.9 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that under a hypothetical shock of a 200 basis point parallel rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Figure 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and commence balance sheet normalization, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management. Figure 5.10 Impact of Interest Rate Shock on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks In the second half of 2017, under a moderate but still favorable economic environment, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed to 5.3% from the strong 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of slowing growth, total loans grew solidly by 16.1% for the full year of 2017. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 0.67% and 0.52%, respectively, compared to 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio also fell to 0.54% and 0.4%, respectively (Figure 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may be more sensitive to external conditions, and therefore banks should closely monitor their credit risk. Figure 5.11 Asset Quality of Retail Banks With banks becoming more optimistic about recent credit growth expectations, strong credit growth is expected to continue. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" for December 2017 showed that 29% of respondent authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk for personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low of 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio for new mortgages further declined to 48.8% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 50.1% in the second quarter (Figure 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio is well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures (i.e., September 2009).

The global economy maintained growth, but uncertainties increased due to persistent trade frictions, tightening financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, leading to a moderation in growth momentum. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," leading investors to rule out further rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to operate smoothly and orderly. In the second half of 2018, total loan growth narrowed slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds such as the ongoing Sino-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with a significant decline in transaction volumes and a fall in property prices, followed by signs of stabilization in early 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector faces multiple headwinds due to increased uncertainties in the external environment. If these uncertainties intensify and persist for an extended period, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks' profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the potential impact of a deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. In the second half of 2018, the global economy maintained growth. However, while the US economy grew robustly, growth momentum moderated in other regions. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major euro area countries experienced slower growth with low inflation. The slowdown in global trade and a significant decline in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In light of the moderating global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, compared to its October 2018 projections. Due to a dimmer growth outlook and escalating trade frictions, global stock markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, raising concerns about an impending US recession. However, the US economic fundamentals remained solid, making a recession in the near term unlikely. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation gives the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's policy stance is data-dependent, suggesting that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as rising US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, it is still unknown whether a "hard Brexit" can be avoided. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilized due to a slowdown in the US dollar's appreciation and market expectations of a Fed pause, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, the weakening momentum of global trade growth has already dragged down economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures have also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma for regional central banks between supporting growth and curbing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private sector debt in some regional countries remain severe. As detailed in Special Topic 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia is that unexpected changes in the Fed's monetary policy could impact sovereign bond markets in emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In Mainland China, growth further moderated in the second half of 2018 due to increased uncertainties in the external environment and a slight slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain amid unresolved Sino-US trade negotiations. A significant contraction in shadow financing activities has led to increased financing difficulties for private enterprises, especially small firms, over the past few quarters, and weakening economic confidence may also pressure business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue balancing economic stabilization and preventing potential systemic risks through accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. At the same time, authorities have also adopted more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among companies of different ownership types, and providing better social safety nets for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%. In 2018, risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets. Bank asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage level of listed non-financial companies edged up. However, bank loan impairment provisions increased further in the second half of 2018, and their exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline, both of which helped protect the banking system from potential credit quality deterioration. Another positive development was that the leverage level of listed companies in overcapacity industries—a major source of bank credit risk—further declined in the first three quarters of 2018. Special Topic 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in business performance of overcapacity industries. Compared with the first half of 2018, Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of the year. GDP growth stagnated on a quarter-on-quarter basis and slowed on a year-on-year basis, dragging full-year economic growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to the direct or indirect impact of the Sino-US trade conflict on consumption and exports. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly reflecting increased economic uncertainties and the wealth effect from adjustments in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong's goods export performance also deteriorated, particularly after the US and China imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Special Topic 3 examines in more detail the impact of the Sino-US trade conflict on Hong Kong's goods trade performance and discusses short-term prospects and related risks. Mainly due to the slowdown in global economic growth, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to slow further in 2019. Under the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, with a low unemployment rate and rising household income, private consumption is expected to continue supporting economic growth, but the outlook for overall investment spending may become more uncertain. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 2% to 3% in 2019, while the latest average growth forecast by private sector analysts is 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the multiple uncertainties and risks mentioned above. Local inflation edged up slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation was partly affected by earlier increases in rents for newly signed local private residential properties. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in over two decades, overall employment growth showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, as the momentum of local economic growth weakens, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2019. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again four times in March 2019 (as of March 19). The Hong Kong dollar rose in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tightening liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered again in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance slightly decreased to HKD 70.9 billion (as of March 19). Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month HIBOR rates rose by about 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% in December (monthly average). Entering 2019, HIBOR rates generally declined due to the fading of seasonal demand. The Composite Interest Rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose from 0.62% at end-June 2018 to 0.83% at end-January 2019. In light of rising funding costs, following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate at end-September, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At end-January 2019, the average mortgage rate for new loans rose to around 2.45%, following the increase in the best lending rate. Due to persistent uncertainties related to the Sino-US trade friction and Brexit negotiations, capital flow volatility may intensify. Moreover, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. In this context, capital outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, due to market concerns over the escalation of the Sino-US trade friction, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates faced depreciation pressure. However, driven by optimism over the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilized in November. Although the Sino-US trade friction persists, it has not yet had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System remained at a high level, further rising to RMB 1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite concerns over the Sino-US trade friction, with the opening of Mainland China's capital account, the development of stock and bond connect schemes, and the promotion of regional economic cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to continue to expand. The local stock market experienced a roller-coaster ride over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply due to the continued tightening of US monetary policy, significant differences in Sino-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in Mainland China. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Fed shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance, while during the trade war ceasefire, China took more measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its market to foreign investors. Although the US filed a highly politicized legal case against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides showed friendly gestures, indicating a determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local stock market rebounded sharply at the beginning of this year. However, as the two sides discuss the details of any agreement, the future remains highly uncertain, and the future development of the US federal government's case could complicate the situation, particularly in the high-tech sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields fell, and near the end of the year, market expectations of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalization strengthened, leading to improved performance. As a result, bond fund flows reversed and increased slightly in the second half of the year. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi market issuance rebounded significantly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total issuance still fell short of maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remains challenging, and its outlook depends on global economic developments, particularly in Mainland China.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but the momentum weakened under the combined influence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly pronounced in regions outside the United States. In light of the fading growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience", and ceased providing forward guidance on further rate hikes. As the Fed's policy stance becomes data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases and may perceive monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty in global trade policy and geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since the end of 2018, due to signs of a slowdown in the US rate hike cycle and a stabilising US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown as the external environment deteriorates, namely the unresolved Sino-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum further decelerated in the second half of 2018, and uncertainty over the growth outlook increased amid the Sino-US trade conflict and financing difficulties for small enterprises. Consequently, policymakers adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. Facing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to contain systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, while the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of a slowdown emerged. There were also clear indications of moderating growth momentum outside the US. Several country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automotive emission standards in Germany, a spike in Italian government bond yields due to a fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France, all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). Additionally, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). A sharp drop in oil prices in Q4 also presented new challenges for commodity-exporting emerging market economies. Given the moderation in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund in January downgraded its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5%. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers' Indices for Selected Advanced Economies Chart 2.2 Global Import Volume and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies In Q4, global equity markets underwent a significant correction, driven by the slowdown in global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed's rhetoric that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry about an imminent US recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-Year and 3-Month US Treasury Yields and Probability of US Recession Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term remains low. The US economic fundamentals remain solid, particularly a tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have only turned positive last year, making it less likely that an overheating economy would force the Fed to tighten monetary policy aggressively. However, possibly considering the significant tightening of financial conditions since Q4, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data-dependent and noted that subdued inflationary pressures allowed them to maintain "patience" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. Furthermore, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further rate hikes and announced it "would be prepared to adjust any details of the balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments." This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World ex USA Index, and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the recent "dovish" signals from the Fed, the outlook for US monetary policy remains highly uncertain, depending on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressures have been subdued so far, giving the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that "patience can be maintained" (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainty. Given these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-Based and Survey-Based Measures of US Inflation Expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically suggests that inflation could pick up in the future (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that essentially rule out any Fed rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average Hourly Earnings and Core PCE Inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-Implied Probability of the Federal Funds Rate Target Range Remaining Unchanged versus at Least One Hike in 2019 In summary, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the Fed is increasingly emphasising that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, especially those that might prompt monetary tightening. Monetary policy at other major central banks is also uncertain. In the euro area, the ECB terminated its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest the full principal of maturing securities purchased under the programme and reaffirming its forward guidance to keep policy rates unchanged at least through summer 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its short-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks to the growth outlook as "tilted to the downside." The impact of this downgraded growth assessment on monetary policy remains to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increased downside risks. However, further monetary easing may face significant headwinds, as its effectiveness is questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining ultra-low interest rates for an extended period are becoming increasingly apparent. For example, due to persistently low yields dragging on profitability, the capital ratio of regional banks has fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. Therefore, the BOJ has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainties related to the global monetary policy outlook, the uncertain outcome of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two major sources of risk for the global economic outlook. In early December, the US government announced it would not increase tariffs on Chinese imports for 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether a long-term trade agreement can be reached remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the EU have made little progress at this stage. As the outcome of these trade talks remains uncertain, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, a disagreement between the two parties over funding for border security led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives could lead to more policy gridlock in the future. In the UK, risks related to Brexit and its knock-on effects surged after Prime Minister May's Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January. Whether a plan can be formulated at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit" remains unknown. Elsewhere, heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the re-imposition of US sanctions on Iran, could also introduce uncertainty to oil prices, thereby affecting global growth prospects. In East Asia, after volatile movements in the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in Q4. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October and signs of Fed patience on further rate hikes eased currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures on East Asian economies. Many regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in Q4, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency Index and Capital Flows Despite stable financial markets, there are increasing signs of a broad-based slowdown in the region. As the Sino-US trade conflict dampened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers' Index for several regional economies, which reflects short-term external trade performance, has fallen into contractionary territory since Q4, suggesting that short-term growth momentum may slow further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit PMI New Export Orders Index for East Asian Economies In an environment of slowing growth and recent declines in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline Inflation Rate and Oil Prices With both recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar being relatively mild, central banks in East Asia have no urgent need to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy trade-off between promoting economic growth and curbing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face challenges from financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

Hong Kong's economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting a slowdown in private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the Sino-US trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is expected to moderate in 2019. The growth outlook for Hong Kong is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019, with potential upside and downside risks to the outlook. Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum seen in the first half, with GDP growth (quarter-on-quarter) turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Year-on-year, economic growth also moderated, with a growth rate of 1.3% in the fourth quarter, below trend growth, dragging the full-year growth rate down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* Based on expenditure-based and seasonally adjusted GDP volume indices. Chart 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to the direct or indirect impact of the Sino-US trade conflict on consumption and exports. Perhaps due to increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect from adjustments in local asset prices, private consumption growth slowed (Chart 3.1). Gross investment spending declined significantly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, especially after the US and China imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports slowed faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Feature 3 will examine Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in more detail and explore short-term prospects and related risks. Chart 3.2 Real Imports and Exports As economic activity weakened, job growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to about 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. With weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no significant signs of improvement. As global economic growth further slows, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Facing a challenging external environment, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, although low unemployment and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to slow, partly due to weaker consumer sentiment and the negative wealth effect from earlier asset price adjustments. Regarding fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily with increased housing supply, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid rising economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index continue to hover in contractionary territory, and their forecasts for future economic growth suggest that year-on-year GDP growth will slow further in the near term. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 2% to 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts from private sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the previous two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures have been accumulating in recent months, they remain mild. Year-on-year, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018, respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, reflecting inflation momentum, has also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rising prices of certain services. The earlier increase in newly signed private residential rentals and the accelerated rise in dining-out prices continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures have remained broadly mild in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Chart 3.4 Rental Component of the Composite Consumer Price Index and Market Rents Chart 3.5 Unit Labour Cost and Per Capita Salary Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019. This mainly reflects the weakening of local growth momentum. However, the earlier rise in private residential rentals will continue to pass through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecasts a mild overall inflation rate of 2.2% for the full year, while the government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remains at around 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market unexpectedly deteriorates, the current near-zero output gap could turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if the Sino-US trade friction eases, leading to better-than-expected local economic performance, it could push up local inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment Rate The Sino-US trade conflict escalated gradually in the second half of 2018: The US imposed 25% tariffs on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China on July 6 and August 23, respectively. Following these two moves, Mainland China responded by imposing 25% tariffs on an equivalent value of US goods. The US further escalated on September 24 by imposing 10% tariffs on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. Subsequently, the two countries engaged in negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as a transit port between these two economies, the tariff increases inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the Sino-US trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This feature reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its short-term prospects. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify trade goods directly affected by the tariff increases, thereby examining the impact of the tariffs more closely. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extract data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports, which are affected by the respective rounds of tariff increases described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the scope of affected goods expanded, covering more consumer goods. For simplicity, we name the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff increases as List 1, List 2, and List 3, respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong's re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. Additionally, readers should exercise caution when analysing data for September 2018, as trade activities in that month were somewhat disrupted by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis results in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff increases. Hong Kong Re-exports Originating from the Mainland and Affected by Tariffs Shortly after the tariff increases, re-exports of relevant goods from Mainland China via Hong Kong to the US appeared to have significantly decreased or slowed in growth (Chart B3.1). For example, the growth of re-exports for Lists 1 and 2 slowed in the first month after the tariff increases, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. Furthermore, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of Goods from Mainland China Re-exported via Hong Kong to the US in 2018 Hong Kong Re-exports Originating from the US and Affected by Tariffs In contrast, re-exports of goods from the US via Hong Kong to Mainland China showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appeared to decrease significantly in the months following the tariff increases but rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 were largely in negative growth throughout the year, while growth for List 3 seemed broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of Goods from the US Re-exported via Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018 Front-loading Due to the time lag between the announcement and final implementation of tariffs (or simply the threat of tariff increases), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected tariff effective dates. Indeed, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite common. Some private sector analysts also believe that these behaviours were partly responsible for the strong overall trade figures before the tariff increases. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for certain tariff list goods, but this appears to be limited to goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). The growth rates of re-exports for Lists 1 and 2 both increased in the months before their respective tariff effective dates. On the other hand, the growth rates of re-exports from the US via Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) show no clear evidence of significant front-loading by businesses. Hong Kong Re-exports Not Affected by Tariff Increases It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the tariff increases account for only about 4% to 5% of Hong Kong's total re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by the tariff increases. We find that re-exports not affected by the tariff increases recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Additionally, the growth of re-exports affected by tariffs (red line) has declined more significantly since the third quarter, reflecting the notable impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in the growth of re-exports not affected by tariffs partly reflects a broader weakening of external demand. As uncertainties persist due to ongoing trade friction, global financial conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand may come under broader pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has dampened global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in adjustments in major stock markets. Import demand from other economies has thus been affected, suppressing Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong's Re-exports in 2018 Even if the Sino-US trade friction eases, the short-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further dampen Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that businesses of all sizes are pessimistic about their business prospects (Chart B3.4), with sentiment particularly low in the trade sector. Other trade-related industries, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business Prospects Survey for Hong Kong's Import and Export Sectors

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades as liquidity tightened due to anticipated seasonal demand for funds. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar gradually weakened, partly due to corporates repatriating funds raised from new share offerings and the market rebuilding carry trade positions, triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Despite this, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong interbank interest rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal demand for funds, before retreating in January 2019. Looking ahead, capital flows in Hong Kong dollars may become more volatile amid uncertainties such as the ongoing Sino-US trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. If the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US remains wide, market carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and potentially triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until March 2019, when the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking a total of four times (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tightening liquidity, but then gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November, driven by the unwinding of carry trades as year-end demand for funds tightened liquidity. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates repatriating funds raised from new share offerings and the market rebuilding carry trade positions. As the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trade activities of buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, leading to a gradual weakening of the Hong Kong dollar, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued smoothly and orderly. The Aggregate Balance has remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and after the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, it slightly decreased to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). The funds that have flowed out of the Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion that has flowed in since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly followed the movement of the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small, thus having a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates The latest balance of payments statistics show that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased stock market volatility, the outflow of equity securities investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the inflow of equity securities investment by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, capital flow volatility may intensify amid uncertainties such as the ongoing Sino-US trade frictions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates may stimulate arbitrage activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the continued normalisation of US interest rates and the multiple triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the monetary base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance slightly decreased to approximately HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, the growth rate of money supply generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HK M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year but only increased slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As a major component of HK M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits remained largely unchanged compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to a decrease in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit rates were raised. An analysis of corresponding assets shows that the slowdown in HK M3 growth was due to changes in banks' capital and reserves (included in "other items net"). Chart 4.5 Changes in HK M3 and Its Corresponding Assets Foreign currency deposit growth accelerated in the second half of the year. US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half of the year, driven by increased deposits attracted after banks raised their preferential US dollar deposit rates, thus becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew slightly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits of authorised institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% growth in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit Growth Although the Hong Kong dollar monetary base and deposit size remain large, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal demand for liquidity occasionally pushed up short-term interbank interest rates, making them more volatile than long-term interbank interest rates (Chart 4.7). The average 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates in December were 2.32% and 2.74% respectively, about 30 basis points higher than the average in June. Entering 2019, as seasonal demand subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally declined. The average 3-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates in February fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly following the movement of the US dollar yield curve. Relative to the end of June 2018, the yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Mortgage Rate for New Loans During the review period, the Composite Interest Rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the Composite Interest Rate increased from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before retreating to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In response to rising funding costs, following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September, retail banks raised their best lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to their best lending rates. On the other hand, the average mortgage rate for new loans rose in line with the best lending rate, standing at approximately 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trend of US dollar interest rates, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as new share subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills, which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds from the Discount Window, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of intensified Sino-US trade frictions, both the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, driven by optimism following the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore renminbi and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates The ongoing Sino-US trade frictions have not yet had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate was mostly below 4% during the review period, with occasional increases due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The 3-month offshore renminbi interbank offered rate hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how the progress of Sino-US trade talks will affect liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 Overnight and 3-Month Offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate Fixing Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half of the year to RMB 657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% growth in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 5.2% in the second half compared to 4.5% in the first half. Among these, the growth rate of corporate customer deposits was faster than that of individual customer deposits. However, the balance of certificates of deposit further declined by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to a reduction in the issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively large number of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Mainly benefiting from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared to the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks rose significantly but remained at relatively low levels. Against an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to persistent uncertainties in Sino-US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, an uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact of a further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared to the same period in 2017, while the return on assets also rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the rise in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For the full year of 2018, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, and the return on assets increased from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks The net interest margin of retail banks further widened to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared to 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank Hong Kong dollar liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018.
