Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time deposit rates to secure longer-term stable funding, Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. Furthermore, following the US interest rate decision at the end of September, banks raised their best lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest Rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period average figures for newly approved loans. At a broader level, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of Hong Kong licensed banks continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of banks rose by 36 basis points, compared to an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks The cumulative increase in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate has outpaced the rise in the overall funding costs of Hong Kong banks, which may have a positive impact on retail banks' Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate-based mortgage loans, which the industry has been actively promoting in recent years. However, the improvement in net interest margins may become more limited in the future, as most Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate-based mortgage loans have reached the cap rate based on the best lending rate. Given the unclear timing of future increases in the best lending rate, the ongoing upward trend in banks' funding costs amid US interest rate normalization may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, increased uncertainties in the external environment may cast a shadow over banks' earnings prospects. In particular, against the backdrop of a slowing global economy, persistent uncertainties in Sino-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. If this leads to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong, well above international minimum standards. As of end-2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capital Position of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions 1. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.0% as of end-December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Category 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable for 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainties in the Sino-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and a slowing global economy, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to a slowdown in the growth of local loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared to growth of 5.3% and 5.2%, respectively, in the preceding six months. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" for December 2018 showed that 82% of all surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of authorized institutions expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to a slowdown in the growth of personal loans (including credit card advances and other loans for personal use), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal GDP growth was slower than the growth in personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has simultaneously impacted both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to mitigate the economic shock of the pandemic, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and local environment, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and monetary markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, loan growth slowed in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, albeit with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking industry will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the rising corporate leverage and personal debt burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios if these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth showed initial signs of stabilisation, benefiting from increased monetary policy easing by major central banks, easing Sino-US trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a "no-deal Brexit" by the UK. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has sparked market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have sharply cut interest rates and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid rising credit spreads and sharp declines in stock markets, global financial conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will impact global economic activity, with the extent of the economic shock depending on the severity and duration of the pandemic. In the medium term, tensions between the US and its major trading partners may reignite, and UK-EU trade negotiations after Brexit could prove challenging. Weak global demand continues to drag on economic growth in the East Asia region<sup>1</sup>. Exports from East Asia to major destinations such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region have recently reported revenue growth, but whether there will be a broad-based rebound in the tech product cycle remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the first phase of the US-China trade agreement announced in December 2019, with the trade truce to some extent reducing global trade uncertainties. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has sparked concerns that the region's economy could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region may hit Asia's tourism industry, particularly economies that rely more on tourism service exports. Due to the region's close supply chain linkages with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019, weighed down by weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the first phase of the US-China trade deal helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties for the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain due to the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and a global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 prioritised stabilising the economy in 2020 while also focusing on financial risk control. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced declining shareholders' equity in recent years, seen as a sign of a "retreat of the private sector." Feature 2 examines the drivers of changes in industrial enterprise equity in Mainland China using 2018 listed company data, finding that private enterprises or small firms are not inherently more prone to downsizing or "retreat." While the study identifies negative profits as the biggest driver, other factors, particularly structural ones, also warrant attention (see Feature 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP continued to decline over the past three quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weak domestic demand, particularly a decline in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely impacted consumer activity, leading to a weak economic outlook and, in turn, dampening consumer and business confidence. Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish, amid renewed Sino-US trade frictions, a global economic slowdown, and a sharp downturn in visitor arrivals. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To allow banks greater room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, on 14 October, the HKMA announced a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent coronavirus outbreak adding substantial downside risks. As industries such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the outbreak will deliver a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash handout to adult permanent residents and a 100% government-guaranteed low-interest loan under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme<sup>2</sup>. On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, allowing banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the first phase of the US-China trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the short term<sup>3</sup>. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (e.g., tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while growth forecasts from international institutions and private sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including a global economic slowdown, Sino-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with a decline in total employment, a rise in the unemployment rate, and a year-on-year decline in the real wage index. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further. Feature 3 will discuss recent developments in the labour market and its short-term outlook in greater detail. Local inflationary pressure continued to build until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. With weak economic conditions, consolidation in private residential rents, and moderate imported inflation, inflation is expected to moderate in the near term. The market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased demand for Hong Kong dollars related to equities (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further, partly due to strong IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened near the end of the year. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading continued smoothly and orderly, with no triggering of the Convertibility Zone. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Feature 4 examines how market attention to future IPO activities affects the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the cap on rates linked to the prime lending rate, the average mortgage rate for new loans rose to around 2.6% in October, but due to reductions in the market prime lending rate from November, the average mortgage rate for new loans edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of a potential further deterioration of the coronavirus outbreak amid external uncertainties. With Hong Kong's substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system, the HKMA has the capacity, resources, and determination to respond to capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, amid market expectations of a US-China trade deal, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened, but came under depreciating pressure from late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the later part of 2019, the offshore renminbi was generally at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with the discount briefly widening at end-January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool rebounded slightly after a minor decline in the previous review period. As of end-January 2020, renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other renminbi business in Hong Kong also grew, with strong growth in local renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement business. The average daily transaction volume of the renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System for the full year of 2019 remained at a high level of RMB 1,133.9 billion. Despite external uncertainties, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of Mainland China's capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, leading the market to anticipate a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide dashed hopes of a recovery, deepening investor concerns about a global recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand in the second half of 2019 cast a shadow over the prospects of regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag on regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism sector particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continues to face challenges from weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has temporarily reduced external uncertainties, downward pressures persist amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by the authorities will provide some buffer. Amid ongoing trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth was sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, growth showed initial signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Figure 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing measures by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Figure 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index However, since late January, the rising number of coronavirus infections globally and the subsequent economic shock have sparked market concerns, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Figure 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays a key role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities in Mainland China and the drag on its economic growth will generate significant spillover effects, potentially impacting the entire globe (Figure 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose direct risks to local economic activity. 5 Figure 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Figure 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China as a Percentage of GDP for Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 In response to the potentially severe economic impact of the pandemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets continue to face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financial conditions, which in turn may exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Beyond the pandemic's development, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to go smoothly, prolonging uncertainties post-Brexit. Additionally, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to weak global demand. Exports from East Asia to major destinations, including the US, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Figure 2.5). Although there are initial signs that the downturn cycle in the region's technology products is bottoming out, including reports of improved earnings at the end of 2019 from some major electronics companies in the region6, it remains to be seen whether a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports will materialise. Figure 2.5 East Asia: Exports of Goods to Major Destinations Remain Weak Weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Figure 2.6), potentially affecting the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in a mild inflation environment, central banks in Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea cut policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after reductions in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand cut its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Figure 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Due to travel restrictions imposed by many regional economies on Mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit first and hardest, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more severely affected by the pandemic (Figure 2.7). The prolonged and intensified pandemic will also impact supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Figure 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the short term, the pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these impacts may be temporary, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and spread of the pandemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations suggest corporate earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Figure 2.8), loose global monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Consequently, regional stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Figure 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for the region's private sector to service debt. While lower local interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Feature 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of private sector debt overhang may also increase, although this effect may be limited to companies with sounder financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowings. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks from the increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress in the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, trade tensions between the two countries persist due to fundamental trade issues. The widening trade surpluses of several regional economies with the US (Figure 2.9) suggest that multinational corporations, seeking to avoid tariffs, may continue to diversify supply sources beyond the China-centric supply chain. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately USD 167 billion. If trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, these Asian economies could become the next targets of trade disputes; for example, the US government imposed tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In light of this, despite the trade truce between China and the US, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Figure 2.9 Trade Surplus in Goods with the US Over the past decade, increased integration of international financial markets has led to a significant rise in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also funds that actively manage based on reference investment indices.9 By introducing overseas investors that would otherwise not be attracted to or engaged with the relevant economies, these funds help develop the financial markets of emerging market economies. Thus, such funds diversify the investor base of emerging market economies, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really a free lunch? For passive bond funds, there are concerns that such fund investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, leading to high leverage levels for these companies.10 Additionally, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by common factors, more vulnerable.11 This feature assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability by examining these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investments to bonds based on the weight of constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds may reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, this behaviour may encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage has risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weights of companies in a major index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as a proxy for their bonds being invested in by passive bond funds,14 we find that an increase in such investments raises the long-term (but not short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The blue solid bars in Figure B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the expanded long-term bond investor base driven by passive bond funds also benefits the development of companies in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effect is only significant for companies with sounder fundamentals, particularly those with stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios (green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent companies do not appear to fall further into a debt trap due to passive bond fund investments. In summary, the above research suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investments may not significantly increase solvency risks in the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Due to weakening private consumption, declining investment spending, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. The economic outlook for 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent coronavirus outbreak also posing notable downside risks. The economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including global economic slowdown, Sino-US trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance, and developments in local social incidents. Given the various economic headwinds, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, though the outlook faces both upside and downside potential risks. Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the full-year economy contracted by 1.2%, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018 and marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis. Figure 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components On a quarter-to-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters, respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, leading to a significant contraction in private consumption starting from the third quarter.33 Due to increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 Externally, with escalating Sino-US trade frictions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals to Hong Kong, the city's external trade performance continued to be sluggish (Figure 3.2).35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in service exports, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance. Figure 3.2 Real Imports and Exports Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, protect employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely impacted industries such as retail, catering services, transportation, and tourism.36 To provide banks with greater room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the recent outbreak also posing notable downside risks. As some industries have yet to recover from the damage caused by social incidents, the outbreak will deliver a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises, especially SMEs, including a one-time cash payment to adult permanent residents and a 100% government-guaranteed special low-interest loan for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.37 On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, allowing banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, particularly for industries and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the outbreak. Analyzed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in previous chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 by February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly concentrated in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, given the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to rise further. Feature 3 will provide a more detailed analysis of recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labor market. Figure 3.3 Labor Market Conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index (CPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the growth rate easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, also eased from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflationary momentum was due to reduced price pressures across several CPI components. For tradeable goods, underlying food inflation remained significant due to rising fresh pork prices, but price pressures for consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, as the growth in newly signed private residential rentals slowed, the growth of the rental component in the CPI also showed a declining trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at moderate levels in recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Figure 3.5 Composite CPI Rental Component and Market Rentals Figure 3.6 Unit Labor Costs Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the short term. Domestically, the weak economic conditions and the widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rentals continue to slow, the housing rental component in inflation should further moderate. Externally, with weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2020 ranges between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5% and an overall inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (e.g., due to the persistence of the coronavirus outbreak), it could further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if the disruption to fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it could exert upward pressure on inflation. Although Hong Kong's economy slowed markedly, the unemployment rate remained at a low of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only with the persistence of social incidents that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this feature analyzes recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market remained broadly stable in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing) and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly due to the costs of adjusting labor demand, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Figure B3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate On the labor demand side, although the Sino-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in trade, retail, and tourism-related sectors, some major industries were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economic recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained stable, and financial activities such as fintech development and new stock listings were very active. These factors may have helped support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. Additionally, the public administration, social, and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many industries is highly correlated with real GDP, the public administration, social, and personal services sectors respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even during an economic slowdown, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected cyclically. Figure B3.2 Changes in Employment by Industry in 2019 On the labor supply side, the labor force participation rate40 fell from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, with the significant economic contraction in the second half, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment decreased during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Figure B3.3 Factors Contributing to Changes in the Unemployment Rate Some structural changes in the labor market are also worth noting. In particular, the increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportion of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment has declined to 6% and 1%, respectively, in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017).42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time workers. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the higher proportion of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further increasing in December, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to remain on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar partly stemmed from stock-related demand and partly from the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions due to tightening liquidity near the year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although the coronavirus epidemic may trigger market sentiment and lead to increased capital flow volatility amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong has substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand capital outflow pressures without affecting its financial stability. Supported by increased stock-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including from initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar further intensified, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly due to buoyant IPO activities and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions as liquidity tightened near the year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly followed the movement of the US dollar, edging up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small, thus having a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates When measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of capital flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. Hong Kong dollar capital flows focus on the currency dimension of capital flows, helping to assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows focus on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps to assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of capital flows require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar capital flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars from banks upon request, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months, so no significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. When there is a large outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflow. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus epidemic on Hong Kong's monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks arising from the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic. Hong Kong has substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remained large, rising by 4.0% from end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at approximately HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued currency notes and coins, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the monetary base During the review period, the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicator remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HK$ M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and then edged up by 0.2% in the seven-month period since end-June 2019. An analysis of counterpart assets shows that the growth in HK$ M3 since end-June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (due to an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins) (Chart 4.5). In the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of HK$ M3) remained largely unchanged (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposit interest rates. Chart 4.5 HK$ M3 and changes in counterpart assets In the seven-month period since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with Renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment-related activities), the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits of authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates experienced volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the active IPO activities in the Hong Kong stock market. The Hong Kong dollar overnight interbank offered rate showed greater volatility in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally rose. Subscriptions for large IPOs put significant pressure on the overnight interbank offered rate. Special Topic 4 provides empirical analysis showing that market attention to future IPO activities also affects the 3-month Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate. This situation can occur if market participants anticipate the future subscription deadline for large IPOs and prepare medium-term funds in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward following the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate, and average mortgage rate for new loans At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected the continued upward adjustment of preferential deposit rates by banks to attract deposit funds, leading to a rise in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. At end-October 2019, following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate, several retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the best lending rates of retail banks are currently in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. For mortgage loans, in the case of mortgage loans benchmarked to the Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rate, major banks raised the interest rate cap determined by the best lending rate, so the average mortgage rate for new loans rose to around 2.63% in October. 45 With the reduction in market best lending rates since November, the average mortgage rate edged down to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus epidemic to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates follow US dollar interest rate movements over the long term, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates may be affected by local factors that could influence Hong Kong dollar demand, such as local IPO activities. Since the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, the sensitivity of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates to changes in the supply and demand of Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment and settlement. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. Should there be a short-term liquidity shortage, banks can use the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Given the potential escalation of the Sino-US trade conflict, the offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore Renminbi against the US dollar falling to a decade low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations of resumed Sino-US trade negotiations reversed the depreciation trend, and the offshore and onshore Renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter, briefly breaking through the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US. However, since late January, due to the outbreak of the coronavirus epidemic, the offshore and onshore Renminbi have again faced weakening pressure. The offshore Renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore Renminbi for most of the period from May to August, and generally at a premium later in 2019, with the discount briefly widening at end-January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore Renminbi exchange rates Despite the volatility in the Renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore Renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate continued to hover between 3-4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced temporary volatility in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share adjustment, and near the Lunar New Year holiday at end-January 2020.

Due to increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of Hong Kong's banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the same period in the review period. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions both increased. However, given the stable level of the aggregate balance of the banking system and broadly stable deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios under the potential intensification of these risk factors. In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased slightly by 1.5% compared to the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks both increased, leading to a slight decline in profitability. Figure 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Although the US federal funds target rate was cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure. On the contrary, affected by multiple local factors (including seasonal funding demand, liquidity demand from large initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions), short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, during the review period, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates remained broadly stable, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate staying at 2.43% as of the end of 2019, close to the level six months earlier (blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained near zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the rate cuts after the US lowered its policy rate. On the other hand, due to the tightening of Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funds. Reflecting the increase in the weighted cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, but remained at a low level by historical standards (green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest Rates From a more comprehensive perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding cost of Hong Kong licensed banks offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of Hong Kong licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Figure 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, providing support to the banking sector's profitability in the same period. Figure 5.4 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Cost and Maturity of Licensed Banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book framework. The overall funding cost and maturity have been calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profitability outlook. These factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of Sino-US trade relations, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors could dampen already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist, which may put pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies in the future, it could worsen the outlook for credit demand and bank asset quality. In terms of overall market development, with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority granting eight virtual banking licenses, Hong Kong's banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks' operations, the long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Thematic 5 show that the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability levels. The capital adequacy of Hong Kong's banking sector remained sound and well above minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Figure 5.5 Capital Adequacy of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, the Basel III non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement is in place to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of Class 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Class 2 institutions also increased moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicates the stability of authorized institutions' funding positions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of Class 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.8), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of Class 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the applicable statutory minimum of 75% for 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. As of the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits in total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.10), as Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits edged down during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies of all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the same year. Given that the aggregate balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have been broadly stable, there were no clear signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Figure 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that under a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in both Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks Against the backdrop of tensions in Sino-US trade relations, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half of the year. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to a moderation in the growth of both local loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the review period. Local loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the growth rates of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the full year of 2019 rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% recorded for the full year of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hope for economic reopening, boosting global growth prospects. Coupled with sustained fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have repeatedly hit new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies is expected to be uneven. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-term economic scars from the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar traded near the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking against the US dollar, mainly driven by stock-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand due to the recurring pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, but still recorded a modest increase for the full year of 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of corporates and households, and the banking industry should closely monitor the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but growth slowed again from the fourth quarter as COVID-19 infection numbers rose. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, supporting a return to normalcy and faster global economic growth. Combined with sustained fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets reached new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. The widespread distribution of vaccines remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier, ending financial markets' expectations of "lower-for-longer" interest rate policies. In the long run, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the pandemic's economic legacies, including high global debt and long-term economic scarring. In East Asia, supported by a rebound in export demand, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows to the region recovered, and yield-seeking activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with weakening fiscal positions in the region, could sour market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually normalized. For the full year of 2020, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains highly dependent on the pandemic's evolution and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecast suggests that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months in early 2020 but then strengthened for the remainder of the year, driven by a faster economic recovery, a weak US dollar, and strong inflows into the Mainland bond market. Detailed research shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (see Box 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in domestic demand and further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that the economy contracted for two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector shows that consumption and tourism-related industries contracted more severely than the overall economy under the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist industries and individuals affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off electronic consumption voucher of HK$5,000 and a 100% government-guaranteed special loan scheme for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme until October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to restore economic activity to normal, the local economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (full year), but the strength and pace of the recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the pandemic's evolution and the rollout and efficacy of vaccines. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support to Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programs. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while international institutions and private sector analysts project average growth of 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high, while the underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. In response to the worsening labour market, the government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund (e.g., one-off grants) to further support industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the short term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021. The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, remained low in recent months despite some fluctuations. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, Hong Kong's inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild in the short term, particularly as the slowdown in rental growth for newly signed private residential leases continues to dampen local inflation. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2021 is a moderate 1.4%, while the government forecasts underlying and overall inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded near the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking against the US dollar, mainly driven by stock-related demand, including from active IPO activities and southbound inflows via Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained brisk in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HK$263.3 billion flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. In total, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic's evolution, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow fluctuations. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance due to the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained at very low levels. The Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021. Due to lower funding costs, the average mortgage rate for new loans also declined from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) strengthened, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, still moderate by historical standards.
