Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit reaching RMB 826.3 billion by end-January 2021. As for other renminbi business, Hong Kong's renminbi bank loans decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew. The average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement System remained high at RMB 1,191.5 billion for the full year of 2020. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border capital flow channels connecting to the Mainland. With the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by a global stock market rally and active buying of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors via Stock Connect, Hong Kong's stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. The global stock market rally was driven by unprecedented monetary easing in major economies; optimism over positive vaccine developments, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activity; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period, and briefly broke through the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing significant net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows to the local market rebounded as market confidence quickly recovered following unprecedented economic stimulus measures by governments worldwide. Despite a modest rebound in bond yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually end and global economic growth to accelerate thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, pushing financial markets to new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of financial markets are out of step with the still challenging macroeconomic environment. If the economic recovery is weaker than expected, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (e.g., due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the dilemma of when to withdraw policy support and must address the many issues left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties from the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, with slower-growing emerging market economies in the region potentially facing greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programs could reverse current optimism, leading to instability in capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumer activities gradually normalized. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely depending on the development of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Consequently, the government announced it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by economic reopenings, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of COVID-19 infections has risen again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, weakening the global growth momentum. At the end of 2020, the emergence of more transmissible virus variants, which subsequently spread worldwide, exacerbated the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use by the end of 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, leading to a return to normalcy and accelerated global economic growth. Another factor supporting the global economic recovery is sustained policy stimulus, including major central banks' commitment to "lower for longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Correspondingly, the International Monetary Fund upgraded its global GDP growth forecast for 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts, January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, with stock prices of cyclical sectors typically benefiting from economic recovery rising, driving global stock indices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). Figure 2.2: 12-Month Forward P/E Ratios of Major Stock Indices However, the strong performance of financial markets contrasts with the still challenging macroeconomic environment. This disconnect could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of controlling the pandemic depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, global vaccination rates were still low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms (e.g., COVAX) aim to promote fairer vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply is expected to exacerbate the low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies. If pandemic control falls short, social distancing and other restrictive measures may need to continue, thereby dampening the global recovery outlook. Figure 2.3: Proportion of Population Receiving at Least One Vaccine Dose in Selected Economies (as of March 15, 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets is based on sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, due to the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have risen (Figure 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Figure 2.4: US and Eurozone 5-Year/5-Year Inflation Swap Rates Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding future US-China relations. The trend of US-China "decoupling," particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the pandemic outbreak. Given the increasingly tough stance of both US political parties toward Mainland China, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in US-China tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing these measures too early could jeopardize the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," these measures are costly in the long run, including fiscal burdens and delays in necessary post-pandemic resource reallocation, such as allowing "zombie companies" with no longer viable business models to survive with continued government support. Additionally, policymakers must address the many issues left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending (Figure 2.5). Although the problems from the rapid debt increase may not be imminent given current extremely low global interest rates, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5: Global Debt as a Share of GDP Another lingering issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may lead companies to reduce investment, and workers who have been unemployed for a long time may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of 2020 after a sharp decline in the second quarter (Figure 2.6). The economic recovery was mainly driven by a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand for electronics and technical equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service industries (e.g., tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact) continued to struggle. Figure 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP Growth in 2020 Despite uncertainties in the economic recovery, portfolio investment inflows have resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields compared to advanced economy bonds (Figure 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccination programs, equity inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly due to portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding about 10% from its low in March last year. Figure 2.7: East Asia: Portfolio Investment Flows East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainties from the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope for the region's hard-hit service industries and economies, competition for early vaccine batches worldwide has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacity. Consequently, slower-growing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism is largely driven by vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls significantly short of expectations, current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices could end. A sudden halt in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With the successful containment of COVID-19 and a gradual recovery in consumption, the Mainland Chinese economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports maintained growth, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (e.g., medical supplies, high-tech products) (Figure 2.8). Over the course of 2020, despite the unprecedented shock of the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Figure 2.8: Mainland China: Contribution of Demand Components to GDP Growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland Chinese economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the economic recovery still depends to some extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in Mainland China have normalized, the service industry continues to face some disruptions as outbreaks reappear in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to new waves of outbreaks in most developed economies. Additionally, US-China tensions may not ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and the concluded EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI) could help further integrate China with other economies, potentially partially offsetting the adverse impact of US-China decoupling on economic recovery. Considering the still uncertain economic outlook, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining macro leverage stability and local government debt sustainability. Furthermore, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long term, the "14th Five-Year Plan" prioritizes technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy, aiming for per capita GDP to reach the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment capacity of bond-issuing companies appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland Chinese bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, due to a significant increase in defaults on state-owned enterprise (SOE) bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds in 2020 increased (Figure 2.9). While the rise in SOE defaults primarily reflects the central government's determination to break the "rigid repayment" of SOEs to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space for some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly in less developed regions. Figure 2.9: Mainland China: Onshore Bond Default Volume and Ratio In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, especially for some higher-risk issuers. Although the ongoing economic recovery and gradual normalization of interest rates partly contributed to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: Mainland China: 5-Year Corporate Bond Yields In the real estate market, housing prices in Mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, price increases in lower-tier cities were much slower (Figure 2.11). The housing oversupply issue that plagued third-tier cities in previous years was largely under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales in these cities amid high market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels, Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, driven by a recovery in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports. With the hope that COVID-19 vaccination will restore economic activities to normal, the Hong Kong economy is expected to return to growth in 2021 after recording its worst contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the Hong Kong economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild. Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the whole of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that it has contracted for two consecutive years, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector also show that economic activity in most sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with the contraction in consumption and tourism-related sectors being worse than the overall economy. On a quarter-to-quarter comparison, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a decline that had lasted for five consecutive quarters (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, but consumer confidence remained weak amid the re-imposition of social distancing measures during the third and fourth waves of the local epidemic. With a temporary improvement in business sentiment, overall investment spending also grew in the second half of the year. Partly benefiting from stronger exports, especially to Mainland China, Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Services trade remained weak as global tourism remained stalled. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting that the recovery in goods exports was slower than that of imports. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the distribution of one-off electronic consumption vouchers of HK$5,000 and a 100% guaranteed personal special loan scheme for the unemployed. The government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for the whole of 2021, while international institutions and private sector analysts forecast average growth of 4.4%. After the end of the "Employment Support Scheme", the government introduced other targeted measures under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund (such as one-off grants) to further support industries hard hit by the epidemic. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation dynamics, has remained at a low level in recent months, albeit with some fluctuations. Specifically, price pressures for basic food have moderated, and the cost of dining out has decreased significantly, reflecting that more restaurants have offered takeaway discounts during periods of dine-in service restrictions. Price pressures for other tradable goods (such as durable goods) remained mild.
