Chart 3.5 Rental Component of Composite CPI and Market Rents Chart 3.6 Unit Labour Costs As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be dampened by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly signed private residential rents. The market consensus forecasts overall inflation of 1.4% in 2021, while the government forecasts underlying inflation of 1% and overall inflation of 1.6% in 2021. With the COVID-19 pandemic wreaking havoc, inbound tourism has rapidly fallen into a slump, and there are concerns that this crisis could have scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this feature empirically analyses the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, thereby exploring the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism in Hong Kong has experienced significant ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals decreased during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Since the launch of the "Individual Visit Scheme" (IVS) in July of the same year, the number of visitors began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply for one to two visits per year as individuals, each stay not exceeding 7 days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009, allowing eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for a "multiple-entry" Individual Visit endorsement (one endorsement for multiple visits) for one year. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased significantly. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure connecting Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a record high in late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events halved the number of visitors in the second half of 2019, and under the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor Arrivals and Related Policies Using the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the launch of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock, as it was largely exogenous in timing and its introduction was not anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our main analysis data comes from population data from the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the catering, retail, hotel and transport sectors. First, we adopt a "difference-in-differences" analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20-40) belonging to the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) belonging to the "comparison group". We classify the younger group as the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. Since the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market can change over time, we also adopt an "event study" approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older group, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries was notably significant and persistent, remaining at around 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (relative to the average difference in the probability of entry for the older group) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the income of workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that after the implementation of the IVS, the income growth of workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and less educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher and increasing income gains (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on Female Employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the Income of Female and Less Educated Workers These results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and less educated workers. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, which showed that the strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled workers, improving the robustness of the labour market for the lower-skilled tier. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to bust, these worker groups may be more affected and deserve close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade near the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related fund demand, including from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and southbound inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HKD 450 billion, Hong Kong interbank interest rates fell across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations could exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system are capable of withstanding the pressures from capital flow fluctuations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related fund demand, including from buoyant IPO activities and southbound inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were repatriated, the Hong Kong dollar traded in a narrow range between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December, as the local stock market sentiment turned positive and market expectations of rising fund demand near year-end. With continued active fundraising activities in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HKD 263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HKD 193.1 billion at end-August to HKD 457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with cumulative inflows of HKD 383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without any abnormal capital flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Equity Funds Raised on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar broadly followed the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar, the trend of the real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations could exacerbate capital flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (e.g., IPOs), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and sound banking system are capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance due to the multiple triggers of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking. Meanwhile, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, resulting in a significant rise in Hong Kong dollar broad money (HKD M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at end-2020. In January 2021, HKD M3 increased sharply again, mainly driven by large IPO activities at end-January. Overall, over the seven-month period since end-June, HKD M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of IPO activities at end-January, HKD M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. By counterpart asset analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HKD M3 was mainly due to the increase in the monetary base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (Chart 4.7). As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of IPO activities at end-January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits of Authorized Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 Changes in HKD M3 and Counterpart Assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since end-June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding IPO activities at end-January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (e.g., seasonal and IPO-related fund demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), and therefore should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong interbank interest rates remained at very low levels overall during the review period (Chart 4.8). Although there were large IPO activities in the second half of 2020, Hong Kong interbank interest rates did not experience significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Interest Rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly followed the trend of the US dollar yield curve, steepening during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared to end-June, the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Mortgage Rate for Newly Approved Loans Retail-level Hong Kong dollar interest rates mainly declined in line with Hong Kong interbank interest rates. The Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, further declined from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Due to lower funding costs, the average mortgage rate for newly approved loans also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly following the trend of the 1-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the best lending rate of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low level of US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened since end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China compared to other parts of the world and the weakness of the US dollar. Following FTSE Russell's announcement at end-September to include Mainland Chinese government bonds in the World Government Bond Index, investment demand further supported the renminbi's strength. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate experienced temporary fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand near year-end, it mostly stayed below 4% (Chart 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate followed the onshore renminbi interest rate, declining in late December and then rising again in late January, partly due to tight onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-Month Offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate Fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of renminbi deposits accelerated, to some extent reflecting the appreciation of the renminbi and higher interest rates on the renminbi relative to other currencies. Compared to end-June 2020, the combined balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the balance of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong Regarding other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion over the seven-month period since end-June 2020. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, the transaction volume handled by local banks reached RMB 3,769.5 billion, an increase of 16.7% year-on-year. Among related transactions, the growth in remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was higher than that of remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong's large renminbi funding pool is sufficient to continue supporting substantial renminbi payment and financial transactions. In 2020, the average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared to RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Due to the recurring COVID-19 pandemic leading to a sustained economic downturn, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks saw further declines in profitability and a slight deterioration in asset quality in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound, supported by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficulties, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may fuel hopes that the global pandemic could be brought under control and economic activities could resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions could adversely affect business activities and continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, the pandemic may weaken the repayment capacity of corporates and households, and the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of these downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared to 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.2), leading to a reduction in net interest income that outweighed a slight increase in non-interest income, resulting in lower profitability. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Figure 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Figure 5.3). The Composite Interest Rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Figure 5.3). The decline in the Composite Interest Rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Figure 5.3 Interest Rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain due to considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capitalisation of Hong Kong's banking sector remains sound and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Figure 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.5 Capitalisation of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Figure 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of Class 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of Class 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The most recent ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicated a stable funding position for authorized institutions. The average NSFR of Class 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of Class 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.8), well above their statutory minimums of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Figure 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as of the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, compared to 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Figure 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point parallel rise in both Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks Against the backdrop of a sustained economic downturn due to the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive growth, albeit with the growth rate slowing significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions decreased by 1.8% in the second half of 2020, following a 3.0% increase in the first half of 2020 (Figure 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Specifically, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with increases of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the preceding six-month period. Figure 5.12 Loan Growth By currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared to the level at the end of June, after decreasing by 2.0% in the first half. Foreign currency loans, which had grown significantly by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand was slightly more optimistic than six months earlier. The HKMA's Credit Conditions Outlook Survey for December 2020 showed that the proportion of respondent authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and companies, banks' loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of loan quality deterioration moderated in the second half of 2020. The overall classified loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the overall classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Figure 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy showed weakness, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify in various regions, especially in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks, and if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected, the pace of monetary policy tightening may exceed expectations. If the Federal Reserve significantly tightens monetary policy, leading to tighter global financial conditions, it will pressure the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could significantly impact the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued smoothly and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth of total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the sustained economic recovery, and the normalization of US monetary policy may proceed faster than expected; these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with weakness persisting into 2022, due to increased mobility restrictions worldwide from the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant, coupled with persistent supply bottlenecks constraining production. At the same time, amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the United States. Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices could further exacerbate global inflation threats, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties. In the short term, if a large-scale pandemic outbreak occurs, the re-imposition of lockdown measures and further deterioration of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has turned hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing reducing its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity, and disorderly capital outflows could pressure the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could pose a sustained upward risk to global commodity prices, exacerbate shortages of industrial supplies, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Special Topic 1 discusses whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during market stress, and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the momentum temporarily slowed in some Southeast Asian economies due to the re-imposition of strict pandemic control measures in the third quarter, while technology product exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new virus variants remain a concern, especially for economies with lower vaccination rates and strained public health resources in the region. Second, the accelerated policy normalization by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and increase currency depreciation pressures; economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, the slowdown in major economies, coupled with the potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed into regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalization decisions of regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in economies with weaker growth momentum and higher sensitivity to energy prices in inflation will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Special Topic 2 examines the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. In Mainland China, economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, impacted by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, due to the persistent downturn in the real estate market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term. Consequently, the Mainland authorities have made stabilizing growth the top priority for this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Total onshore bond defaults in the second half of 2021, including defaults by state-owned enterprises on onshore bonds, decreased. Special Topic 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remains controllable, as Mainland banks, especially systemically important banks, have limited exposure to developer loans, with low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but at a slower pace compared to the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately, as goods exports and private consumption benefited from the sustained global economic recovery, improvements in the local labor market, and the government's consumption voucher scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local pandemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures have put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with increased maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking sector, has also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering for the full year of 2022, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are affected by various uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalization. As the economy recovered, the labor market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed renewed signs of labor market pressure amid the new wave of local pandemic. Additionally, a decline in the number of online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local pandemic and tightened pandemic control measures will put some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, especially for industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to price increases for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and pandemic-related logistics disruptions, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term. However, weak rents and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2022 is 2.4%, while the government expects overall inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak net buying flows southbound via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen with the Federal Reserve's monetary policy normalization. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained on the strong side of the convertibility zone for most of the time, with trading continuing smoothly and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued smoothly and orderly. Due to ample interbank liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained low during the review period. The average mortgage rate for new loans edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued to grow, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances increasing to RMB 1,113.5 billion by the end of January 2022. Although renminbi loan balances decreased, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System in 2021 rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Looking ahead, leveraging Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way northbound and southbound links under the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of Mainland China's capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global stock markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to hit a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict have led to consolidation in major global stock markets since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of variant viruses (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed significantly in the latter part of 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance to a hawkish one, exacerbating the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and also adversely affecting emerging markets where the recovery generally still lags. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in global financial markets, amplifying some of the aforementioned risks. In Emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with major technology product exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform others. While the Omicron variant is not currently causing a severe disruption to the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the normalization of Fed policy could trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies could weigh on the region's goods export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, leads to higher commodity prices and increased inflation risks, and on the other hand, weakens consumption and increases global economic uncertainty, which will complicate the decision-making of regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalization. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, impacted by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from the cooling real estate market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the government has prioritized stabilizing growth as its top task for this year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to the tightening of mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain issues (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials like semiconductors) continued to pressure production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in January forecast that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China offsetting the expected growth rebound in other parts of Asia (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1 IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the US, which has implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a broad range of goods and services (Figure 2.2). Furthermore, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices of various commodities, which could exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures. Figure 2.2 Core Consumer Price Index Inflation Rates in Selected Economies (1) Latest data for the US, UK, and Eurozone are for January 2022; for others, December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asian Economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Asian Market Economies" include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with downside risks, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions impact global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far taken targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared to previous lockdown policies, these looser measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Figure 2.3). However, in the event of a large-scale outbreak, lockdown measures could be re-implemented, leading to a worsening of supply bottlenecks. Figure 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Delivery Times Sub-Index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief for goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current high global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk of higher commodity prices from the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia, the lagged pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the potential for earlier sharp rises in global residential property prices to drive up rents later, upward risks to wage growth from tight labor markets, and rising inflation expectations. Notably, with US inflation recording its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterizing high inflation as "transitory," and doubling the pace of asset purchase reductions from $15 billion to $30 billion per month to end the asset purchase program by March 2022, while beginning discussions on reducing the balance sheet. In fact, recent market pricing suggests the Fed may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs given the Eurozone's closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine. In this context, coupled with persistently high global debt levels and asset valuations under prolonged accommodative policies, if inflationary pressures persist and require the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, it could worsen borrowers' debt servicing capacity and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, with escalating geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of a US dollar shortage have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. In the event of a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Feature 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during market stress and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Figure 2.4). Meanwhile, South Korea and Singapore, as major exporters of technology products in the region, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the uneven recovery across the region. Additionally, inflationary pressures in many Emerging Asian economies remained moderate. Figure 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index The market generally expects a broad recovery in Emerging Asia in 2022, but the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread in the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than previous waves of infection; however, some regional economies with still lagging vaccination rates and tighter public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, Fed policy normalization could trigger capital outflows and put depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Figure 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in US long-term yields could also spill over to Emerging Asian long-term bond yields, exacerbating the risk of adjustment in regional asset markets. Figure 2.5 Correlation of Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields with Corresponding US Treasury Yields Third, the outlook for regional goods trade faces headwinds from slowing major economies and uncertainty about a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which could dampen the region's export growth. Figure 2.6 US: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will feed into regional inflation while also weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making of regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalization will become more complex. Central banks in regional economies with weaker growth momentum and greater sensitivity of inflation to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder for regional economies of the long-term need to rebuild a more sustainable and resilient growth model to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced significant outflows (Figure B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Figure B1.1 Fund Outflows from Some Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Event In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the large outflows could be investors taking "first-mover advantage" by redeeming early to avoid bearing the potentially sharply rising redemption costs during market stress. To curb outflows driven by first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds use swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical research on whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this feature conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing reduced outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 event, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. Additionally, this feature will identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will offer policy recommendations regarding financial stability. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming earlier than other investors, thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. First-mover advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, where the costs of subscription and redemption by fund investors (e.g., transaction costs from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund price after the transaction. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to expectations of rising redemption costs. This amplifies the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open-ended funds.

With sustained growth in goods exports and private consumption, Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, recording its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local epidemic and the tightened social distancing measures imposed accordingly put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activities. The overall economy is expected to maintain a recovery for the full year of 2022, but its strength and pace will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the epidemic and the normalization of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labor market outlook, which had improved significantly in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term due to rising import prices, weak local rents and labor costs should contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year comparison, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), but the growth rate moderated compared to the first half of the year. For the full year of 2021, real GDP grew by 6.4%, the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Figure 3.1 Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components On a quarter-to-quarter comparison, economic activities grew moderately by 0.6% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Figure 3.1). Domestically, improved labor market conditions, coupled with the government's consumption voucher scheme, drove up private consumption. However, overall investment spending declined in the final quarter after a strong rebound in the previous two consecutive quarters. Externally, as the global economy continued to recover, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained strong, while services trade remained weak, partly due to the continued stagnation of inbound tourism (Figure 3.2). On a net basis, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Figure 3.2 Import and Export Volumes The new wave of local epidemic and the tightened social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activities in early 2022. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking sector, also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue to recover for the full year of 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are affected by numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the accelerated normalization of US monetary policy, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if Hong Kong resumes quarantine-free travel with Mainland China earlier than expected, it could stimulate local economic growth. With the economic recovery, the labor market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year (Figure 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent low in February 2021, but remained below the pre-epidemic level. In early 2022, official data showed renewed pressure on the labor market amid the new wave of local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local epidemic and tightened epidemic prevention measures will put some pressure on the local labor market (especially industries involving face-to-face contact) in the short term. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Figure 3.3 Labor Market Conditions Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year comparison, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualized underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, with the recovery of local demand and rising external prices (Figure 3.5), the prices of dining out and some energy-related items have accelerated. At the same time, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Figure 3.6). Although real unit labor costs remain weak, they have risen slightly in recent quarters, partly due to some improvement in real average wages (Figure 3.7). Figure 3.4 Different Indicators of Consumer Price Inflation Figure 3.5 Hong Kong Import Prices Figure 3.6 Composite Consumer Price Index Rent Component and Market Rents Figure 3.7 Unit Labor Costs Looking ahead, with rising import prices and logistics disruptions due to the epidemic, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term. However, weak rents and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for overall inflation in 2022 is 2.4%, while the government forecasts overall inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% in 2022.

Under the hedging sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. Due to ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, Hong Kong interbank offered rates remained at low levels. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system to withstand the impact of capital flow fluctuations. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone for most of the time, with trading continuing smoothly and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid hedging sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 due to improved market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak net southbound buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned hawkish. During the review period, IPO fundraising activities continued to support the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Net Southbound Buying through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity Funds Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable due to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility. With rising US dollar interest rates, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds (the speed and scale of which will depend on market conditions at the time) could lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the Weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without affecting financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base rose by 1.4% in the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' sustained demand for such bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before discount window operations) correspondingly decreased by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued currency notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes In the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be affected by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment-related activities), so it is advisable to observe longer-term trends. For the full year of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits of Authorized Institutions by Currency Overall, trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Due to ample liquidity in the banking system, Hong Kong interbank offered rates remained low despite market concerns over US monetary tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of increased funding demand near year-end, Hong Kong interbank offered rates edged up in December 2021. The average loan rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system provides sufficient buffer during large capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand near year-end, the overnight offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate experienced slight volatility in late December 2021, while the 3-month offshore renminbi Hong Kong interbank offered rate remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and 3-Month Offshore Renminbi Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate Fixing In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi funding pool continued to grow steadily. In the six months since end-July 2021, renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong During the six-month period since July 2021, although renminbi loan balances decreased by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, Hong Kong's renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. From end-July 2021 to end-January 2022, the transaction volume handled by banks in Hong Kong reached RMB 3,763 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% compared to RMB 3,181 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's large renminbi funding pool continued to support substantial renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the full year of 2021, the average daily turnover of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement System rose from RMB 1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Renminbi Trade Settlement Remittances Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way northbound and southbound Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the Mainland's capital account, increased demand for renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalation of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic developments led the Hang Seng Index to fall to a near two-year low at end-February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening asset market sentiment and a new wave of the local pandemic. Major global stock markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). Supported by the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings amid government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, the uptrend in major global stock markets was sustained, but the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, with growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, at end-2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global markets. The Hang Seng Index fluctuated between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at end-2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic developments and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low of 22,713 points at end-February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Due to the emergence of the highly contagious Omicron variant, stock market implied volatility fluctuated significantly in late November 2021 before subsequently retreating. Although the skew index fell from its historical high in late June 2021, it remained at elevated levels, reflecting investors' concerns about a correction in the long-term stock market rally since the pandemic outbreak, leading them to allocate more funds to hedge against downside risks (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option Implied Volatility of Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and Skew Index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong stocks continued to record net capital inflows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, southbound trading through Stock Connect recorded significant net capital outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of Mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, buying through southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording a total capital inflow of HK$98.3 billion by end-February. Over the review period, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net Capital Inflows into Hong Kong's Stock Market Chart 4.14 Net Flows through Stock Connect Mechanisms After reaching a record high in the first half of 2021, Hong Kong's primary market slowed in the second half of the year. For the full year of 2021, there were 98 new IPOs, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), a 17.8% decrease in total funds raised compared to the previous year. In 2021, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange ranked fourth globally in the public offering market, behind Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong IPO Market The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. The easing of Mainland monetary policy and more secondary listings of Chinese concept stocks in Hong Kong's primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic developments, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The specific classification loan ratio edged up in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. With sound capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, the HKMA extended a number of relief measures to further assist the economy through difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could threaten the economic recovery, coupled with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected, both of which will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak earnings performance was mainly attributable to a decline in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Figure 5.1). For the full year of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% from 2020, while the return on assets fell from 0.77% to 0.59%. Figure 5.1 Retail bank profitability Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA's issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills, Hong Kong interbank offered rates edged up in the final quarter of 2021. However, given the still very ample liquidity in the banking system, interbank rates remained at relatively low levels. Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (see the blue line in Figure 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. The Composite Interest Rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds of retail banks, rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (the green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period average figures for new loans approved. (c) Starting from June 2019, the Composite Interest Rate has been calculated in accordance with the newly implemented local "Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book" framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those for earlier months. From a broader perspective, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong rose slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4 Funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars Starting from June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks continue to submit returns under the existing Interest Rate Risk framework. The overall funding cost has been calculated as a weighted average of the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those for earlier months. While US monetary policy normalisation may signal an improvement in bank profitability, the improvement in the near term could be partially offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve has indicated multiple rate hikes in 2022, past experience suggests that changes in local interest rates may lag behind those in US interest rates (especially when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very ample). Therefore, it may take more time for an improvement in banks' net interest margins to materialise. In addition, a surge in Omicron variant cases could introduce uncertainty to the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impacts. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report last year, we have for the first time published the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document this year. I hope this report will provide readers with a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable organisation. Over the past year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's key functions. Readers will learn about our specific measures and efforts in this report, with the following highlights: Banks face climate risks in their daily operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks' resilience to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into the supervisory process and explored the use of technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. Given the increasing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we have shared good practices with the industry on managing these products effectively, thereby promoting banks' ability to strengthen their climate risk management. The HKMA actively participates in collaborative initiatives addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will enhance transparency in financial markets and align green finance policies. Internationally, we are actively engaged with various international organisations to help formulate policies addressing climate change and assess their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing.
